overview: Northern Qi was the Gao family dynasty ruling from Ye in northern China between 550 and 577. Its short political life produced ambitious Buddhist sculpture, painted tombs and inventive ceramics, drawing on connections with India, Central Asia and West Asia.

periods.title: Gao Yang establishes Northern Qi
periods.summary: In 550 Gao Yang replaced Eastern Wei with Northern Qi, retaining Ye as the capital.

periods.title: Later courts and conquest
periods.summary: Monumental art continued under later rulers; Northern Zhou conquered the dynasty in 577.

items.text: This outline is a coarse boundary drawn for the atlas after a historical map, not a surveyed frontier. Its 550 to 577 dates describe the Northern Qi dynasty; the eastern state should not be confused with neighboring Northern Zhou.
The Gao court inherited Ye rather than building a capital from nothing. A change of dynasty could leave the seat of government in place while replacing the family at the top.

Excavations at Ye have exposed rammed-earth palace foundations, corridors, enclosing walls and paved routes belonging to Eastern Wei and Northern Qi. Together they reveal how rulers organized movement through connected halls and courtyards, rather than a single isolated palace building.

Beside palace building 209 at Ye, archaeologists found a brick-lined drain about 65 centimeters wide at the top and 35 centimeters deep. Its brick bottom and sides show deliberate water management. This palace drain does not establish that every home had plumbing.

At Ye’s Northern Qi Dazhuangyan Temple, building 9 retained white plaster and traces of red paint. Brick-and-tile paths linked nearby spaces, including three roughly four-meter-square rooms whose precise functions remain uncertain. Excavation turns a lost religious complex into walls, surfaces and walkways people actually used.

sections.title: Making useful things and memorable pictures

items.text: Caocun, east of Ye’s inner city wall, was a pottery-production area during Eastern Wei and Northern Qi. Excavators uncovered three kilns, glazed pottery, celadon and kiln furniture. These firing supports are workshop equipment: evidence for the practical labor behind attractive finished pots.

A small stoneware jar in the Metropolitan Museum carries applied musicians and floral decoration beneath a celadon glaze. Just 18.1 centimeters tall, it is attributed to Northern Qi. The museum connects its applied decoration with Central Asian traditions: international influences could fit on a tabletop.

Xu Xianxiu’s tomb at Taiyuan, dated 571, includes a north-wall banquet image of the owner and his wife, with musicians and attendants nearby. It presents an elite family’s imagined afterlife. The scene is valuable evidence for status and entertainment, not a picture of every family’s dinner.

One musician in Xu Xianxiu’s tomb has hands positioned to play a flute, but the flute itself was never painted. Geng Shuo identifies this small omission among signs of hurried work. Even an impressive ancient mural could have an unfinished detail hiding in plain sight.

The painted wife in the same tomb has traces of two versions of her right eye. An earlier small eye was replaced with a longer one. This is an artist’s revision, not unusual anatomy, and it helps researchers reconstruct the sequence of painting.

At Lou Rui’s Northern Qi tomb, painters first marked outlines with bamboo while the lime plaster was still soft. Some final brush lines moved away from those guides. Surviving horse outlines let researchers see the difference between the draft and the finished design.

sections.title: Families, learning and an unexpected bathroom clue

items.text: Writing sample: 我有一兒，年已十七 means “I have a son, already seventeen years old.” Yan Zhitui records a Northern Qi father’s words in chapter 2 of his Family Instructions, completed later in life. This is a modern Chinese text edition, not a surviving sixth-century manuscript.

That father taught his son the Xianbei language and pipa playing to win favor with high officials. Yan disapproved of this career strategy. The anecdote links language and music lessons with an ambitious household’s hopes.

Yan describes brothers sharing a table, handing down clothes, studying together and playing together. This affectionate picture supports his ideal of sibling loyalty; it is advice in his later book, not a survey of every Northern Qi household.

Yan also recalls women at Ye managing households, pursuing lawsuits and seeking posts for sons. He disapproved of their public activity. His complaint nevertheless preserves evidence of women doing considerably more than staying quietly at home.

Later, Yan refused to reuse paper bearing revered writing for unclean purposes. Historian Roel Sterckx calls this an indirect early toilet-paper reference. Even recycling had literary rules! It does not date the invention of toilet paper.

At Xiangtangshan, Buddhist scriptures were carved into cave walls. A surviving text from the South Cave of the Northern Group dates to about 572 to 577. Stone offered durability when paper and silk were fragile, and believers feared that Buddhist teachings might be lost.
Later rubbings copied those inscriptions onto paper: an inked pad darkened the surface while recessed characters remained white. Copies carried the carved writing away from the cave for study.

Many Xiangtangshan sculptures were removed for the art market in the early twentieth century. A research project begun in 2004 used three-dimensional scans of scattered fragments and cave surfaces. Matching breaks and chisel marks helps reconstruct where pieces once belonged, like an enormous archaeological jigsaw.

ending.text: Northern Zhou conquered Northern Qi in 577, ending the Gao dynasty’s rule and reuniting northern China under its rival. That political defeat did not erase the region’s people: its buildings, objects and written recollections preserve lives extending beyond the dynasty.
